clinicalPearls: A severe, usually autosomal recessive red cell membrane disorder within the hereditary elliptocytosis spectrum, caused by defects of the spectrin cytoskeleton (commonly alpha-spectrin, SPTA1) with reduced membrane mechanical stability

Typically presents in infancy or early childhood with moderate to severe haemolytic anaemia, jaundice and splenomegaly, and is easily mistaken for hereditary spherocytosis or non-immune neonatal haemolysis
The blood film is striking, with marked poikilocytosis, red cell fragmentation, microspherocytes, elliptocytes and bizarre budding forms, and a very low MCV
Red cells show abnormal thermal instability, fragmenting at a lower temperature (around 45-46 degrees Celsius) than normal cells, which resist to about 49 degrees, the historical basis of the name

HPP frequently coexists with hereditary elliptocytosis in a kindred: a parent may have mild or asymptomatic elliptocytosis while the child has severe disease, reflecting a compound state or a low-expression alpha-spectrin allele (such as alpha-LELY) in trans
The molecular defect usually involves the spectrin self-association site, destabilising the spectrin tetramer that maintains membrane integrity
Management is supportive with transfusion in early life, and splenectomy can substantially reduce haemolysis in severe transfusion-dependent cases
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis results from qualitative and quantitative defects of spectrin, most often mutations in alpha-spectrin (SPTA1) affecting the spectrin self-association domain, frequently combined in trans with a low-expression allele that reduces spectrin production. Because spectrin tetramers form the horizontal scaffold of the red cell membrane skeleton, these defects weaken membrane cohesion; red cells lose surface area, fragment under shear and thermal stress, and adopt bizarre poikilocytic shapes with microspherocytes. The mechanically fragile cells are prematurely destroyed in the spleen and circulation, producing chronic haemolysis with a markedly shortened red cell lifespan.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary elliptocytosis, the milder related disorder
Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia or thermal-burn red cell fragmentation
Neonatal non-immune haemolytic anaemia of other cause
Hereditary stomatocytosis and other membrane disorders
Unstable haemoglobin or red cell enzymopathy
additionalInvestigations: Blood film review with red cell morphology and MCV (characteristically low)
Reticulocyte count and markers of haemolysis (bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin)
Eosin-5-maleimide binding flow cytometry and osmotic fragility, recognising overlap with hereditary spherocytosis
Thermal stability testing of red cells, showing fragmentation at a reduced temperature
Red cell membrane protein analysis by gel electrophoresis with spectrin studies
Molecular testing of SPTA1 and SPTB and related membrane genes, with family studies
Direct antiglobulin test to exclude immune haemolysis
redFlags: Severe neonatal haemolysis with anaemia and hyperbilirubinaemia risking kernicterus
Transfusion-dependence with faltering growth in infancy
Aplastic crisis precipitated by parvovirus B19
reference.prognosis: With supportive care the haemolysis often lessens after infancy, and splenectomy markedly reduces transfusion needs in severe cases, so the overall outlook is generally good. Lifelong monitoring for gallstones, iron status and haemolytic or aplastic crises remains necessary.
pitfalls: Labelling the infant as hereditary spherocytosis and missing the underlying spectrin defect
Overlooking a parent's mild elliptocytosis that clarifies the inheritance
Attributing the fragmented film to a microangiopathic process and pursuing an unnecessary work-up
Proceeding to splenectomy without vaccination, thromboprophylaxis awareness and appropriate age considerations
Missing coexisting iron overload or pigment gallstones on long-term follow-up
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Transfuse red cells for symptomatic anaemia, particularly during infancy when haemolysis is most severe
Consider splenectomy to reduce haemolysis and transfusion dependence in severe disease, preceded by appropriate vaccination and followed by antibiotic prophylaxis against encapsulated organisms
Supplement folic acid to meet the demands of chronic haemolysis
Monitor for and manage pigment gallstones, transfusional iron overload, and haemolytic or parvovirus-triggered aplastic crises
Manage neonatal jaundice with phototherapy or exchange transfusion where required
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with kindred studies for coexisting hereditary elliptocytosis
